title: Voice of the customer survey: what it can and cannot tell you
summary: Voice of the customer surveys measure prevalence, not cause. Learn when surveys work or fail, and how to pair them with interviews for decision-ready findings.
body_markdown:
Does a voice of the customer survey replace qualitative research, even with open-ended questions? +


No. Surveys measure prevalence, how widespread a sentiment or behavior is. Explaining why it exists takes a different instrument. Adding open-ended questions doesn't change that without follow-up probing: unprobed responses stay at the level of sentiment ("it was confusing") instead of becoming a traceable, reconstructed experience a team can act on. That's what conversational, AI-moderated research is built for.


How often should a voice of the customer program run? +


Wave-based, for example every two weeks or monthly. Conveo StoryLines is built around this continuous cadence.


What makes VoC findings actionable instead of landing in a deck? +


Traceability. Every theme needs to link back to a specific participant, timestamp, and source recording, so a stakeholder who questions a finding can see the evidence instead of taking it on faith. Without that link, even valuable feedback gets treated as anecdote.


Is a consistent question taxonomy necessary across survey waves? +


Yes. Without consistent wording for recurring themes, cross-study trend analysis breaks down and teams end up rediscovering the same pain points every quarter instead of tracking whether interventions work.


What is the difference between a relationship survey and a transactional survey? +


A relationship survey, most often built around net promoter score, measures the overall state of a customer relationship at a point in time. A transactional survey, most often built around a customer satisfaction score or customer effort score, measures a single support interaction or purchase moment. Effective VoC surveys usually run both, since each captures a different slice of the customer experience.
